simulationRules: Great powers act on plausible post-2016 interests. Honor the historical friendships, rivalries, and red lines described in the world briefing unless in-game events credibly change them. Economic weight, energy, alliances (NATO, EU), and nuclear status all shape what each polity can realistically attempt. Keep escalation gradual: open conflict between major powers requires sustained provocation, not a single move.
startingTimelineText:
World briefing — 1 January 2016. History is factual through this date; everything after is a divergent timeline.

UNITED STATES — Federal republic, roughly 240 years old, the world's sole superpower with unmatched military, financial, and technological reach. Built on liberal-democratic ideals, free markets, and global alliance networks. Pivoting attention toward the Asia-Pacific while still entangled in the Middle East. Friends: NATO, United Kingdom, Japan, South Korea, Israel, Australia. Rivals: Russia, China (strategic competition), Iran, North Korea.

CHINA — A civilization-state with several millennia of cultural continuity, now the rising industrial superpower under one-party rule and a state-guided economy. Prizes sovereignty, internal stability, and the long game; expanding influence through trade, infrastructure, and naval reach in the South China Sea. Friends: Russia (pragmatic alignment), Pakistan, North Korea, Cambodia. Rivals: United States, Japan, India, Vietnam.

RUSSIA — Heir to the Russian Empire and the USSR, a security-obsessed nuclear power that leverages energy exports and military force to defend a sphere of influence. Recently annexed Crimea (2014) and is intervening in Syria. Friends: China, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Syria, Iran. Rivals: NATO, United States, Ukraine, Poland, Baltic states.

GERMANY — The economic engine of Europe and anchor of the European Union and the euro. Post-war pacifist tradition, export-driven industry, cautious military posture. Currently managing a large refugee inflow. Friends: France, EU partners, United States, NATO. Rivals: none open; friction with Russia over Ukraine, sanctions, and energy dependence.

FRANCE — Nuclear-armed permanent UN Security Council member and co-leader of the EU with Germany. Assertive military abroad (Sahel, Levant) and recently struck by terrorism at home. Friends: Germany, EU, United States, NATO. Rivals: jihadist networks; competitive friction with Russia.

UNITED KINGDOM — Nuclear power and global financial hub, close US ally, debating its place in the EU ahead of a 2016 referendum. Strong intelligence and expeditionary capability. Friends: United States, NATO, Commonwealth, EU (for now). Rivals: Russia; strategic competition with China.

JAPAN — Advanced economy and key US ally in Asia, constitutionally pacifist but rearming amid regional tension. Friends: United States, Australia, India, South Korea (uneasy). Rivals: China, North Korea, Russia (Kuril dispute).

INDIA — The world's largest democracy, a rising nuclear power balancing non-alignment with growing ties to the West. Friends: Russia (legacy defense ties), United States (warming), Japan, Bhutan. Rivals: Pakistan, China.

ITALY — Founding EU member and Mediterranean power on the front line of migration flows. Friends: EU, NATO, United States. Rivals: none open.

IRAN — Revolutionary Islamic republic and regional Shia power, just entering the post-sanctions period after the 2015 nuclear deal. Projects influence via proxies across the Levant and Gulf. Friends: Russia, Syria, Hezbollah, Iraqi factions. Rivals: United States, Israel, Saudi Arabia.

SAUDI ARABIA — Oil-rich Sunni monarchy and guardian of Islam's holy sites, anxious about Iran's rise and leading an intervention in Yemen. Friends: United States, Gulf monarchies, Egypt, Pakistan. Rivals: Iran, the Houthis.

ISRAEL — Advanced, militarily dominant state in a hostile neighborhood, undeclared nuclear power, deeply tied to the United States. Friends: United States; quiet alignment with Gulf states against Iran. Rivals: Iran, Hezbollah, Hamas.

TURKEY — NATO member bridging Europe and the Middle East, increasingly assertive under a strong executive and central to the Syrian war and refugee crisis. Friends: NATO (strained), Qatar, Azerbaijan. Rivals: Syria's government, Kurdish militias; tense with Russia after a downed jet.

BRAZIL — The largest Latin American economy and a regional leader, mired in political and economic crisis. Friends: BRICS partners, regional neighbors. Rivals: none open.

NORTH KOREA — Isolated, nuclear-armed totalitarian state surviving on deterrence and Chinese support, prone to provocation. Friends: China (reluctant patron). Rivals: United States, South Korea, Japan.

SOUTH KOREA — Advanced democracy and US ally under constant northern threat, technological and industrial powerhouse. Friends: United States, Japan (uneasy). Rivals: North Korea.

UKRAINE — Post-2014 state fighting Russian-backed separatists in the Donbas after losing Crimea, seeking closer ties to the EU and NATO. Friends: United States, EU, NATO (support short of membership). Rivals: Russia.
